Theoretical Basis for Length Scaling¶

Overview¶

We assume that the Horton ratios calculated by (Boyd & Allen, 2025) reflect the geomorphic structure of the river network because they were calculated on NHDPlusV2 flowlines, which primarily represent perennially flowing reaches not subject to extension. Because NHDPlusV2 flowlines do not represent the absolute smallest streams in the network (Benstead & Leigh, 2013), Boyd & Allen (2025) extrapolated their calculated Horton ratios to the true hydrologic 1st order. Necessary to this extrapolation is the assumption that the network is scale-invariant: the geomorphic structure of the smallest reaches of the network reflects that of the largest reaches. We make the same assumption.

Consider the Horton ratios from (Boyd & Allen, 2025). $$ n(\omega) = ab^{\omega}$$ $$ \bar{l}(\omega) = cd^{\omega} $$

$ n(\omega) $ represents the number of streams of a particular Strahler order, $ \bar{l}(\omega) $ represents the mean length of the streams of a particular order, and $ \omega $ represents the order. $ a $, $ b $, $c$, and $d$ are fitted constants. For any stream order $ \omega $, the links of $ \omega + 1 $ will be $ b $ times as numerous and have $ d $ times the average length. In practice, $ b = 0.25 $ and $ d = 2.225 $, so $ \omega + 1 $ has $ 1/4 $ times the number of streams of $ \omega $, while those less numerous streams are $ 2.225 $ times the length. This scaling applies across the network irrespective of stream order. As hydrologic conditions change, the network extends or contracts, and stream orders are reassigned. The lengths and abundances of valleys don't change, nor do the locations of confluences. Thus, regardless of whether a set of links is order 3 or order 6, its number and average length scale predictably by the same factor to the next up- and downstream orders.

For convenience, $ n(\omega) $ and $ \bar{l}(\omega) $ can be collapsed into a single law representing total length per stream order. $$ L(\omega) = n(\omega) \bar{l}(\omega) = ac(bd)^\omega = fg^\omega $$ This scaling law is linear in semilog space. The slope is given as $ \log g $, and the y-intercept as $ \log f $. Slope $ \log g $ represents the geomorphic structure of the network and does not vary with flow. Y-intercept $ \log f $ varies with flow. The following behavior is expected:

Flow accumuation thresholds¶

We seek to validate this behavior using two approaches. Necessary to both approaches are flow accumulation thresholds. Corresponding to each of 10 flow deciles, we derive 10 flow accumulation thresholds from the topographic parameters by (Prancevic et al 2025). Catchment network length scales as $L \propto Q^\beta$. We assume that length mapped in NHD corresponds to median discharge from GRADES-DL and fit the $\log(Q) \propto \beta\log(L)$ line through the point $(\log(L_{NHD}), \log(Q_{med}))$ to give a definite relationship between length and discharge: $$\log(L) = \beta(\log(Q)-\log(Q_{med})) + \log(L_{NHD})$$

This relationship is a jump beyond existing literature on stream extension, which has historically focused on $\beta$. We apply this relationship to flow deciles to get length at each flow level. A similar derivation is used to calculate drainage area at the channel head. The $\alpha$ parameter provided by (Prancevic et al 2025) describes how drainage area accumulates in the downstream direction with this relationship: $L \propto A^{-\alpha}$. In other words, moving up the network from valley to hillslope, drainage area goes as a power law of $L^{-1/\alpha}$. We anchor the length-drainage area relationship in a similar way using a known point. The (Prancevic et al 2025) dataset includes values for minimum and maximum calculated drainage density and mimimum and maximum calculated channel head area, which are used in their elasticity analysis. We fit $A \propto L^{-1/\alpha}$ through the point $(L_{max}, A_{min})$ to get the next relationship: $$\log(A) = -(\frac{1}{\alpha})(\log(L) - \log(L_{max})) + \log(A_{min})$$ The decile lengths calculated from the length-discharge equation are fed into the area-length equation to calculate flow accumulation thresholds per catchment per flow decile.

MERIT Hydro network approach¶

For each of 10 flow deciles, we extract river networks from the MERIT Hydro rasters (Yamazaki et al 2019). We assign stream orders and sum the length per stream order. For the lowest stream orders, $ L(\omega) $ scales as expected. At all flows, the $ L(\omega) $ curves have roughly equal slopes. The relationships deteriorate for high stream orders due to (1) finite size effects deflating the abundance of high-order streams and (2) a relatively small number of long streams being dynamically reordered. One drawback of this approach is the spatial resolution of the rasters (90 m). Some per-catchment flow accumulation thresholds derived from (Prancevic et al 2025) produce a network with finer drainage density than can be represented with this spatial resolution. We instead use the median accumulation threshold per flow decile rather than per-catchment values. This approach cannot account for geographic varability in network elasticity or drainage density.

Hydrosheds v2 vector trimming approach¶

Next, we validate the theory by trimming the headwaters from the Hydrosheds v2 vector network. Hydrosheds v2 reaches have a flow accumulation threshold of ~ 1 km2, which is far larger than the derived flow accumulation thresholds. We trim the vector network for each of 10 flow levels. To do this we overlay the catchment polygons with flow accumulation attributes on the network vector product with a drainage area attribute. For each flow decile, the network is filtered to remove reaches whose drainage area is less than 50x the overlying catchment's corresponding flow accumulation threshold. 50x flow accumulation was selected to maximize the available data while still capturing "full" network dynamics. In tests where the network was trimmed by 10x flow accumulation, in many cases the 8th decile network was expected to have a higher drainage density than Hydrosheds v2 offers. The highest-flow networks were expected to be longer than the untrimmed Hydrosheds v2 network. Because this approach does not involve generating any new flowlines (and it cannot until flow accumulation rasters in units of area rather than pixels are released), applying this method with 10x flow accumulation cannot produce network extension across the range of flows.

Though the resultant networks are substantially smaller than those dervied from DEMs, this approach is still valid given the scale-invariance of river networks. The results of this approach are broadly similar to those of the network extraction from MERIT rasters. At low stream orders, $ \log {L(\omega)} $ scales linearly with $ \omega $ with the same slope regardless of flow. The clean relationship breaks down at high orders due to dynamic reordering and finite size effects.

Theoretical stream order assignment¶

The total network length as a function of $ f $ and $g$ is given by $ S = \sum_{\omega=1}^{\omega_{max}} fg^{\omega} $. Network length is calculated per catchment from the (Prancevic et al 2025) dataset by the process described in Flow accumulation thresholds. Total network length is calculated per flow level by summing these catchment network lengths. To implement the theoretical scaling, we optimize $\omega_{max}$ and $f$ so that the summation meets three constraints:

  1. $ g = 0.5565 $ as calculated from the Horton ratios given in (Boyd & Allen, 2025).
  2. The $ L(\omega) $ sum must be equal to the total network length for the corresponding flow decile.
  3. $ L(\omega_{max}) $ must be close to 1879 km, the length of the highest stream order given by (Boyd & Allen).

The conceptual method was developed by a human. The mathematical details of the optimization and the function solve_f_and_n were written by an LLM and checked by a human.

The optimization follows these steps:

Step 1¶

From the given length of the highest stream order, the total length of the network, and the g value, what is the highest stream order in the network? This step does not necessarily produce a whole number because it is highly improbable that each stream order is exactly $g$ times the length of the next and that the sum of the lengths exactly equals the expected total network length. Fractional stream orders don't make sense, so we round the calculated highest stream order to the nearest integer.

Derivation of stream order:

$ S = \sum_{\omega=1}^{\omega_{max}} fg^{\omega} $ is a geometric series. For $ g \neq 1 $, it can be rewritten as $$ S = \sum_{\omega=1}^{\omega_{max}} fg^{\omega} = fg \frac{1-g^{\omega_{max}}}{1-g} $$ The length of the highest stream order is given by $$ Y = L(\omega_{max}) = fg^{\omega_{max}} $$

f is isolated in the equation for the length of the highest stream order. $$ f = \frac{L(\omega_{max})}{g^{\omega_{max}}} $$

f is replaced in the summation. $$ S = g (\frac{L(\omega_{max})}{g^{\omega_{max}}}) \frac{1-g^{\omega_{max}}}{1-g} $$

Simplify. $$ S = L(\omega_{max})\frac{g^{1 - \omega_{max}} - g}{1-g} $$

$\omega_{max}$ must be isolated. $$\frac{S(1-g)}{L(\omega_{max})} + g = g^{1-\omega_{max}} $$

Log pulls $\omega_{max}$ out of the exponent. $$ \log_g(\frac{S(1-g)}{L(\omega_{max})} + g) = 1 - \omega_{max} $$

Highest stream order is given. $$ \omega_{max}=1-\frac{\log(\frac{S(1-g)}{L(\omega_{max})})}{\log(g)} $$

Step 2¶

Then, using the rounded $\omega_{max}$, we calculate $f$ by rearranging the geometric sum as $$ f = \frac{S(1-g)}{g(1-g^{\omega_{max}})} $$ Results of optimizing $ f$ and $\omega_{max}$ follow.

# optimize f and max order to fit known g, length per max order, and total network length
def solve_f_and_n(g: float, S: float, Y: float):
    """
    Solve for f and n given:
        L(omega) = f * g**x,  x = 1, 2, ..., n
        S = sum_{x=1}^{n} y(x)   (known total network length)
        Y = y(n)                 (known value at the highest stream order)

    Returns
    -------
    n_hat   : int     n rounded to the nearest natural number
    f_sum   : float   f recomputed from the sum condition using n_hat (alternative)
    """

    if g <= 0:
        raise ValueError("g must be positive for the log formula to be real-valued.")

    if g == 1:
        # Degenerate case: y(x) = f for all x
        n_exact = S / Y
        n_hat = max(1, round(n_exact))
        f_sum = S / n_hat
    else:
        inner = S * (1 - g) / Y + g
        if inner <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                "Invalid inputs: log argument is non-positive "
                f"(computed inner={inner}). Check S, Y, g for consistency."
            )
        n_exact = 1 - np.log10(inner) / np.log10(g)
        n_hat = max(1, round(n_exact))

        # compute f after rounding n (max order) to integer
        f_sum = S * (1 - g) / (g * (1 - g**n_hat)) if n_hat > 0 else float('nan')

    return n_hat, f_sum

flist = [None] * 10

active_network_order_dfs = [None] * 10


for n in range(len(anl_list)):
    anl = anl_list[n]
    Y = 1_879      # known value at x = n (the last term)
    n_hat, f_sum = solve_f_and_n(g, anl, Y)
    max_order = n_hat
    f = f_sum

    orders = np.arange(1, max_order + 1)
    lengths = f * (g ** orders)
    active_network_order_dfs[n] = pd.DataFrame({'order': orders, 'length_km': lengths, 'Q_decile': np.array([n] * len(orders))})

active_order_df = pd.concat(active_network_order_dfs)

Similarity of scaling¶

Both geospatial approaches produce networks with $g$ values lower than the $g$ derived theoretically from Carter's Horton ratios. 2 separate $g$ values are calculated: one for stream orders 1-5 prior to the takeover of finite-size effects, and the other for all stream orders. The brute-force approaches predict that $L(\omega)$ decays less rapidly with increasing stream order than the Horton ratios from (Boyd & Allen, 2025) predict. The newly calculated $g$ values are close to that calculated from the data in table 2 of (Downing et al 2012). Because Hydrosheds v2 and MERIT both rely on extracting networks from rasters, the lengths of the smallest stream orders are underestimated because the rasters cannot resolve meander bends smaller than their spatial resolution. This also explains why the $g$ values for the MERIT approach are lower than those for the Hydrosheds v2 approach. NHDPlusV2 is built partly from field data and is less likely to suffer from this issue. Regardless, the $g$ values for the brute-force approaches are within the range of published values, and I am confident in their validity.
